entries.topicDescription: Lightweight concurrency primitives at the core of Go.

tips.title: Goroutines are incredibly cheap — use them freely
tips.content:
A goroutine is a lightweight thread managed by the Go runtime.
Starting one is as simple as prefixing a function call with
the 'go' keyword. Each goroutine starts with only ~2KB of
stack space.

Unlike OS threads (which cost ~1MB each), you can easily run
tens of thousands of goroutines concurrently. The Go scheduler
multiplexes goroutines onto a small pool of OS threads.

This makes concurrent programming feel natural. Need to handle
10,000 connections? Launch 10,000 goroutines. Need to process
files in parallel? One goroutine per file.

But remember: goroutines are concurrent, not necessarily
parallel. True parallelism depends on GOMAXPROCS and available
CPU cores.

tips.title: Channels are typed pipes for goroutine communication
tips.content:
Channels provide a safe way for goroutines to communicate
and synchronize. They're typed: a chan int carries integers,
a chan string carries strings.

Sending to a channel (ch <- value) blocks until another
goroutine receives (value := <-ch). This synchronization
is built in — no mutexes needed for the data being sent.

Buffered channels (make(chan int, 10)) allow sends without
an immediate receiver, up to the buffer size. They're useful
for producer-consumer patterns and rate limiting.

Go's motto is: "Don't communicate by sharing memory; share
memory by communicating." Channels embody this philosophy
and prevent data races by design.

tips.title: Select multiplexes channel operations
tips.content:
The select statement lets a goroutine wait on multiple
channel operations simultaneously. It blocks until one
of its cases can proceed, then executes that case.

If multiple cases are ready, select picks one at random.
A default case makes select non-blocking — useful for
polling or try-send patterns.

Select is essential for timeouts (using time.After),
cancellation (using context.Done), and fan-in patterns
where you merge multiple channels into one.

Combined with for loops, select creates powerful event
loops that react to whichever channel has data first.
